title: Unraveling non-monotonic responses of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation to post-2100 global warming
abstract: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) shapes global climate extremes. Although most climate models project its intensification through the 21st century, its behavior beyond 2100 remains unclear. Here, we conducted multi-scenario simulations extending to 2500 with an Earth System Model to assess ENSO responses across different warming levels and analyzed a multi-model ensemble. We find that ENSO amplitude, asymmetry, periodicity, and diversity change non-monotonically: under moderate global warming, ENSO strengthens with persistent positive skewness and ~4-year periodicity. Under extreme global warming, ENSO amplitude and skewness decline, and its period shortens to 2–3 years, favoring Central Pacific events. These non-monotonic changes arise from a shift in the eastern Pacific background from equatorial surface wind divergence to convergence, which promotes ocean heat discharge and efficiently terminates ENSO. Our findings indicate a shift toward more frequent but less intense ENSO variability in a high-warming world, posing challenges for climate projection and adaptation.
problem: The behavior of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) beyond 2100 under global warming remains unclear, as most climate model projections are limited in duration and do not capture its complex, non-monotonic responses to different warming levels.
method: We conducted multi-scenario simulations extending to 2500 with an Earth System Model and analyzed a multi-model ensemble to assess non-monotonic El Niño-Southern Oscillation responses across a wide range of global warming levels.
task: The task is to assess the non-monotonic responses of El Niño-Southern Oscillation characteristics, such as amplitude and period, to different global warming levels using multi-scenario Earth System Model simulations extending to 2500.
innovation: This paper reveals that ENSO's response to global warming is non-monotonic, strengthening under moderate warming but weakening and shortening its period under extreme warming due to a background climate shift in the eastern Pacific from equatorial surface wind divergence to convergence.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: ENSO originates from coupled ocean-atmosphere processes in the equatorial Pacific, develops through Bjerknes feedback, and is terminated by Sverdrup transport, which discharges equatorial upper-ocean heat anomalies to off-equatorial regions¹-5. These processes generate interannual variability in equatorial Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) over a period of 2–7 years”, which, in turn, affects year-to-year global climate.

Another essential aspect of ENSO is its pattern diversity, or flavors, that is, the coexistence of Eastern Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP) ENSO events in observations12,13. Strong El Niño events favor the EP type, whereas strong La Niña events often occur as CP-type events 11,14,15.

We conducted a series of numerical simulations using the Earth System Model MIROC-ES2L40. This model was originally designed to simulate the long-term evolution of climate-biogeochemical processes, which enables both the centennial simulations conducted in this study and simulations on the millennium time scale 52,53. The historical and SSP experiments follow the CMIP6 protocols until 210054-57. The SSP experiments were extended to 2500 following Meinshausen et al.³¹, where fossil and industrial CO2 emissions were assumed to become zero by 2250 to stabilize the radiative forcing. The SSP experiments in this study included eight scenarios: SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP5-3.4-OS, SSP4-3.4, SSP2-4.5, SSP4-6.0, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5.

The schematic (Fig. 9) summarizes a nonlinear transition in ENSO behavior with increasing global warming, associated with contrasting changes in the Pacific background state and the processes that modify ocean-atmosphere coupling. Under moderate warming, weakened eastern equatorial Pacific divergence and reduced zonal SST contrast accompanied by a persistent cold tongue may help enhance the Bjerknes feedback through increased upper-ocean thermal stratification²². This is consistent with strengthened EP and CP ENSO events that coexist with an ~4-year period, producing positive skewness of Niño-3.4 SST anomalies and favoring more extreme EP El Niño events.

Fig. 7 | Amplitude, asymmetry, and period of ENSO in multiple climate models. Twelve climate models of the 5th and 6th phases of the Coupled Model Inter-comparison Project (CMIP5 and CMIP6) are available for the RCP8.5/SSP5-8.5 scenarios extended to 2300. ENSO amplitude (a) is derived as the standard deviation of the ENSO index, ENSO asymmetricity (b) is defined by the variance-weighted skewness of the ENSO index, and ENSO periods (c) are based on the autocorrelations of the ENSO index. Green and purple bars represent the results for 1900–1999 and 2200-2299, respectively.
